title: Fatality inquiry into police shooting recommends more crisis intervention training for officers
subtitle: The need for crisis intervention and de-escalation training for police officers to be mandatory in Alberta is just one recommendation stemming from a fatality inquiry into a 2015 case where a man opened fire on officers in north Edmonton before being shot dead.
article: The need to make crisis intervention and de-escalation training mandatory for police officers in Alberta is just one recommendation stemming from a fatality inquiry into a 2015 case where a man opened fire on officers in north Edmonton before being shot dead.

Michael David Perreault, who had a long history of mental health issues and substance abuse problems, was shot and killed the night of May 18, 2015, by city police Const. Wayne Haltli after his partner, Const. Jeffrey Park, was shot in the leg with a sawed-off shotgun during a traffic stop.

Park and Haltli were members of the city's Specialized Traffic Apprehension Team (STAT) when they responded that night to a 911 report of a suspected impaired driver in the Beverly neighbourhood, says the fatality inquiry report released Tuesday by Alberta Justice.
Perreault's Nissan Maxima had stopped in the curb lane on Victoria Trail near 118 Avenue when the constables approached the driver's side door.
The officers reported that the 31-year-old, who was sweating profusely "as if you had poured a bucket of water over his head," was "belligerent" and "unco-operative."

After Park reached into the car to try to take the keys out of the ignition, Perreault grabbed his arm and tried to pull him into the vehicle. Park punched Perreault in the head several times to no effect before the constables tried to drag the man from the vehicle.
Perreault, splayed across the seats, reached into the front passenger footwell, retrieved a shotgun and aimed it at Haltli.
When he pulled the trigger, the gun didn't fire, but as both officers attempted to reach safety, Perreault got a shot off and hit Park in the lower leg.
Perrault exited the vehicle and was pointing the shotgun at Haltli when he was shot and killed by the officer.

An investigation by the province's police watchdog, the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT), previously found the officers used reasonable force as Perreault "presented a very real and continuing threat" to the officers and the public.

A toxicology report presented to the fatality inquiry found Perrault had high levels of oxycodone in his system, along with methamphetamine and therapeutic levels of two prescription psychoactive drugs used to treat a range of conditions including depression and anxiety.
Perrault, who had an extensive history with the Edmonton city police,  felt "cops hated him" and had singled him out for scrutiny, the report said.
It also notes that Perrault was suffering abnormal behaviour on the day of his shooting and was paranoid that a police officer could be outside his home.
Perrault visited physicians more than 55 times over a 12-month period and was diagnosed as having "chronic narcotic dependent pain syndrome."

In making her recommendations stemming from the inquiry, provincial court Judge Jody Moher said more work still needs to be done to address the opioid public health crisis in Alberta, especially the misuse and diversion of prescription pain medication.
Moher also recommended Alberta police look to other jurisdictions to help guide policies regarding use of force.
Mandatory professional training for police officers should also include crisis intervention and de-escalation techniques, Moher wrote.
